extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, policymakers, and regulators focused on banking, mortgage markets, and fintech
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and quantitative analysis of the rise of shadow banks and fintech lenders in U.S. residential mortgage origination (2007–2015), including data assembly, lender classification, causal identification using geographic regulatory heterogeneity, and a calibrated model decomposing drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of traditional bank vs shadow bank
rubrics_metrics.description: A lender is a “bank” if it is a depository institution; a lender is a “shadow bank” otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is consistent with the Financial Stability Board (FSB) definition: banks = deposit-taking corporations; shadow banks = credit intermediation involving entities and activities outside of the regular banking system. The paper focuses on mortgage origination; whether a non-depository institution has a funding relationship with a depository institution is not the classification focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintech lender classification
rubrics_metrics.description: A lender is a fintech lender if it has a strong online presence and if nearly all of the mortgage application process takes place online with no human involvement; specifically, the loan application process is entirely online and the potential borrower is able to obtain a firm, contractual rate quote without interacting with a human loan officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification focuses on front-end consumer interaction: automated tools that collect/verify information (e.g., employment history) and issue a contractual quote. Having an online form is not sufficient; sites that route applicants to human loan officers are non-fintech. Ambiguous cases are conservatively classified as non-fintech. Multiple independent research assistants verify classifications and the Wayback Machine is used to confirm historical stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lender classification coverage target and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Manually classify lenders so that the classified sample covers 80% of total originations by value in 2010 (551 lenders classified in HMDA; identified 55 unique sellers in Fannie/Freddie data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identification in Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, and HMDA data, manual linking across years to overcome mergers/name changes, and manual checks of regulator labels in HMDA. Use archived webpages and independent reviewers for robustness. Results reported for both full and top-50-lender subsamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of regulatory burden (four specific shocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the impact of four specific increases in regulatory burden: (1) capital requirements (Basel III changes and limits on counting MSRs toward regulatory capital), (2) mortgage servicing rights (MSR) rule changes, (3) mortgage-related lawsuits/settlements arising from the crisis, and (4) the movement of supervision to the OCC following closure of the Office of Thrift Supervision (OTS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory burden is measured using bank call report balance-sheet data (to compute capitalization), timelines and amounts of lawsuit settlements (Law360, SEC, SNL Financial), and institutional changes (OTS closure → OCC). Exploit geographical variation in banks' exposure to these burdens to identify effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference-in-differences identification exploiting geographic heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use difference-in-differences tests exploiting geographical heterogeneity induced by increases in regulatory burden to compare bank and shadow bank lending in counties where banks were more exposed to regulatory changes versus less exposed counties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach aims to avoid confounds related to credit demand differences across counties. The timing of specific regulatory changes is linked to shadow bank rise in exposed counties; tests include county/zip-time fixed effects and loan-level controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and inclusion/exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple datasets: HMDA (mortgage application and originator identity), Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac single-family loan performance (conforming 30-year fixed, full-documentation loans), FHA loan-level snapshots (FHA-insured loans), US Census/ACS (county demographics), bank call reports (balance-sheet capitalization), and lawsuit settlements (Law360, SEC, SNL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of dataset limitations: Fannie/Freddie datasets exclude ARMs, interest-only, balloon loans, government-insured loans, loans not reflecting current underwriting, etc. FHA data lacks borrower FICO. HMDA records whether loan was sold within the calendar year and may misclassify loans sold in subsequent years as 'not sold'. Manually link lenders across years to handle mergers/name changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing and loan disposition metrics (hold vs sale and time-to-sale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether originators retain loans on balance sheet or sell within one year (HMDA), and define Time_to_Sale as quarters between origination and sale (mean ~40 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time_to_Sale is defined in quarters and estimated via regressions controlling for loan covariates and fixed effects. Compare average time-to-sale across lender types (traditional bank, non-fintech shadow bank, fintech) to infer balance-sheet capacity or technological processing differences. Note HMDA 'not sold' may include loans sold in subsequent calendar years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan-level comparison metrics and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare lender types on loan and borrower characteristics (loan amount, term, LTV, DTI, FICO, refinance type, first-time buyer, mortgage insurance) and on pricing/outcomes (interest rates, delinquency/performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regression specifications with borrower and loan controls, zip x quarter fixed effects, and quarter fixed effects. For pricing, report differences in mean interest rates and assess explanatory power of standard pricing variables (FICO, LTV) across lender types to infer differing information usage by fintech firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of fintech pricing informational content
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how well standard variables for predicting interest rates (e.g., FICO and LTV) explain variation in interest rates for fintech versus non-fintech lenders; fintech lenders show substantially less variation explained by these variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret lower explanatory power as fintech using different information (big data, alternative signals) to set rates. Use comparison regressions and R-squared or variance-explained metrics across lender types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and structural decomposition approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Calibrate a quantitative model of mortgage origination with three lender types (traditional banks, non-fintech shadow banks, fintech shadow banks) differing on regulatory burden, convenience, and costs to decompose contributions to shadow bank growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed variation in mortgage rates and market shares to identify parameters; interpret model output to attribute shares of shadow bank growth to regulation (~60%), technology (~30%), and other sources (remaining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative treatment of ambiguous fintech cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Where correct classification is ambiguous regarding fintech status, treat the lender as a non-fintech shadow bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conservative rule reduces false positives in identifying fintech lenders. Classification is done by hand with multiple independent RAs and validated with archived webpages. Sensitivity/robustness checks are reported (e.g., exclusions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of web-archived evidence for temporal classification stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Wayback Machine to view archived webpages to confirm historical accuracy and stability of fintech/non-fintech classifications over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that lenders classified as fintech in 2016–2017 would have been classified the same in 2010; ambiguities (e.g., Movement Mortgage, Summit Mortgage) are discussed and handled conservatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and sensitivity practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform robustness checks including alternative samples (e.g., top 50 lenders), excluding large influential firms (e.g., Quicken Loans), and varying control sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report appendix tables showing results when excluding large lenders, restricting to subsets, and alternative specification choices to demonstrate stability of main findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and measurement caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and report limitations: HMDA's conforming label understates conforming market share due to within-year sale requirement; FHA data lacks FICO; HMDA 'not sold' may include loans sold in later calendar years; dataset exclusions in Fannie/Freddie affect sample representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss these caveats when interpreting financing shares, time-to-sale, and pricing/performance comparisons; where possible, rely on datasets (Fannie/Freddie) with richer borrower controls for rate/outcome analysis.
